questions.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes has glucose 420 mg/dL, beta-hydroxybutyrate elevation, arterial pH 7.22, and potassium 5.6 mEq/L. Which initial management should the nurse anticipate for diabetic ketoacidosis?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Begin potassium replacement before fluids because total-body potassium depletion means serum potassium is always low.","B":"Give IV bicarbonate immediately because a pH of 7.22 requires bicarbonate before fluid and insulin therapy.","C":"Delay crystalloid and insulin until the glucose falls below 250 mg/dL to avoid an abrupt osmotic shift during treatment.","D":"Start IV crystalloid, then insulin with frequent potassium monitoring because the potassium is not below 3.5 mEq/L."}}
questions.rationale: Current hyperglycemic-crisis guidance prioritizes IV crystalloid resuscitation, followed by insulin with close potassium monitoring. Potassium replacement is needed as levels fall, but insulin is delayed specifically when potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L; this client is at 5.6. Bicarbonate is not routine at pH 7.22, and treatment is not delayed until glucose is below 250 mg/dL.
questions.source_name: ADA/EASD/AACE/JBDS/DTS — Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes Consensus Report
questions.source_detail: 2024 consensus: initial crystalloid, insulin therapy, and potassium threshold for delaying insulin

questions.stem: A client with acute kidney injury has potassium 6.8 mEq/L and reports new palpitations and lightheadedness. Which action should the nurse prioritize?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Place the client on continuous cardiac monitoring, obtain an ECG, and escalate the severe hyperkalemia urgently.","B":"Assess bowel sounds first because gastrointestinal motility is the most sensitive indicator of potassium toxicity.","C":"Recheck the potassium at the next scheduled chemistry draw before initiating cardiac monitoring or escalation.","D":"Assess skin turgor and oral intake first because determining hydration status takes priority over cardiac evaluation."}}
questions.rationale: Severe hyperkalemia can cause life-threatening conduction abnormalities and arrhythmias. With potassium 6.8 mEq/L plus palpitations and lightheadedness, cardiac monitoring, ECG assessment, and urgent escalation are priorities. Gastrointestinal or hydration assessments do not outrank cardiac risk, and waiting for a routine repeat level is unsafe in a symptomatic client.
questions.source_name: American Heart Association — 2025 CPR & ECC Guidelines, Hyperkalemia
questions.source_detail: Hyperkalemia section: severe hyperkalemia can cause life-threatening arrhythmias; characteristic ECG abnormalities described

questions.stem: A client reports new crushing substernal chest pressure radiating to the left arm with diaphoresis and nausea. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Administer an antacid and reassess the pain after gastrointestinal causes have been excluded at the bedside.","B":"Have the client ambulate briefly to determine whether the discomfort is reproducible with physical activity.","C":"Place the client on cardiac monitoring, obtain a 12-lead ECG promptly, and activate the acute coronary syndrome pathway.","D":"Delay diagnostic testing until a troponin result is available because ECG findings are not useful before biomarkers rise."}}
questions.rationale: This presentation is concerning for acute coronary syndrome. Immediate cardiac assessment and a prompt 12-lead ECG are central to early evaluation while the ACS pathway is activated. Antacid testing, exertion, or waiting for biomarkers can delay recognition and treatment of myocardial ischemia.

questions.stem: A client arrives 2 hours after onset of a disabling ischemic stroke. Imaging excludes hemorrhage, blood pressure is 178/96 mm Hg, and no contraindication to IV thrombolysis is identified. Which action should the nurse anticipate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Delay reperfusion therapy until the blood pressure is below 160/90 mm Hg, then reconsider thrombolysis.","B":"Prepare for IV thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase because the client is within the 4.5-hour window.","C":"Administer aspirin before any thrombolytic so platelet inhibition is established before reperfusion treatment.","D":"Begin an unfractionated heparin infusion as the preferred reperfusion treatment for acute disabling ischemic stroke."}}
questions.rationale: The 2026 AHA/ASA ischemic-stroke guideline endorses either alteplase or tenecteplase for eligible patients with disabling deficits within 4.5 hours. A blood pressure of 178/96 mm Hg is below the traditional pre-IV-thrombolysis threshold of 185/110 mm Hg, so lowering it below 160/90 solely to qualify is unnecessary. Aspirin before thrombolysis and heparin as a substitute for IV thrombolysis are not the indicated reperfusion strategy.
questions.source_name: American Heart Association/American Stroke Association — 2026 Acute Ischemic Stroke Guideline
questions.source_detail: 2026 guideline: alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours for eligible disabling stroke

questions.stem: A postoperative client has temperature 38.9°C, heart rate 118/min, respiratory rate 24/min, new confusion, and blood pressure 86/50 mm Hg. Which action is the nurse's priority?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Use qSOFA alone to confirm sepsis before notifying the provider or beginning any resuscitation measures.","B":"Administer an antipyretic and reassess in one hour because postoperative fever commonly explains the other findings.","C":"Wait for final blood-culture results before initiating resuscitation or antimicrobial therapy to avoid overtreatment.","D":"Activate urgent sepsis evaluation and resuscitation, obtain cultures and lactate, and prepare timely antimicrobials."}}
questions.rationale: The client has possible sepsis with hypotension and acute mental-status change. The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign emphasizes that sepsis is a clinical diagnosis and a medical emergency: evaluation and resuscitation should begin immediately, with blood cultures obtained as soon as possible, lactate measurement suggested, and timely antimicrobial therapy based on likelihood and shock status. qSOFA should not be used as the sole screening gate, and waiting for final cultures is unsafe.
questions.source_detail: 2026 recommendations: sepsis is clinical diagnosis; resuscitation immediately; cultures/lactate; antimicrobial timing
